## Architecture stack: overview

![source: Perplexity AI](assets/architecture__stack.png)


## Architecture stack: Layer 1 - PHY

Controls **physical layer** (PHY, ,i.e. "radio") aspects[^l1_ref]:

- Radio interface
- Channel coding and modulation schemes.
- MIMO processing and beamforming
- Hybrid Automatic Repeat reQuest (HARQ) buffering

[^l1_ref]: See [5G NTN Stack Architecture](https://gatehousesatcom.com/product/5g-ntn-new-radio/5g-ntn-new-radio-gnodeb/){target="_blank"}

## Architecture stack: Layer 2 - MAC

Controls **Medium Access Control** (MAC, i.e. protocol) aspects of the radio interface:

- Manages scheduling and multiplexing
- Hybrid Automatic Repeat reQuest (HARQ) management and execution:
  - Combine retransmissions to improve reliability and reduce latency.
  - Replay a packet after an error
  - Manage ACK/NACK feedback from the receiver
- For NTN, MAC includes HARQ adaptations for longer round‑trip time (RTT) delays.

## Frequency bands: use cases

- **Lower bands** (narrowband)
  - Good coverage/ubiquity
  - Limited capacity
  - Application: IoT and M2M. Not intended for high data rate applications

- **Upper bands** (wideband)
  - Limited coverage
  - High capacity
  - Application: high data rate applications, dense urban areas and hotspots

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import seaborn as sns
import matplotlib.ticker as ticker # Import ticker module

sns.set_theme(style="whitegrid") # Apply a seaborn style for better aesthetics
plt.rc('axes', unicode_minus=False) # Ensure minus signs are displayed correctly

all_bands = {"FR1-L": FR1_bands_L, "FR1-S": FR1_bands_S, "FR1-Ku": FR1_bands_Ku, "FR2-Ka": FR2_bands_Ka}

colors = {'Uplink': 'skyblue', 'Downlink': 'lightcoral'}

# Helper function to plot bands on a given axis
def plot_bands_on_axis(ax, band_type_names_for_this_subplot, xlim_range, title_text, num_xticks=5):
    current_y_pos = 0
    y_tick_positions = []
    y_tick_labels = []

    # First pass to determine y_tick_positions and y_tick_labels
    for band_type_name in band_type_names_for_this_subplot:
        bands_dict = all_bands[band_type_name]
        for band_name, freqs in bands_dict.items():
            y_tick_positions.append(current_y_pos)

            # Calculate downlink bandwidth for the label
            if 'Downlink' in freqs:
                start_freq_dl, end_freq_dl = freqs['Downlink']
                bandwidth_dl = end_freq_dl - start_freq_dl
                y_tick_labels.append(f'{band_name} ({bandwidth_dl:.1f} MHz)') # Format bandwidth with 1 decimal place
            else:
                y_tick_labels.append(band_name) # Fallback if no downlink specified

            current_y_pos += 1
        current_y_pos += 1 # Add a gap between band types

    # Second pass to plot and add band type labels
    current_y_pos_for_plotting = 0 # Reset for plotting
    for band_type_name in band_type_names_for_this_subplot:
        bands_dict = all_bands[band_type_name]

        for band_name, freqs in bands_dict.items():
            for link_type, (start_freq, end_freq) in freqs.items():
                width = end_freq - start_freq
                # Only add legend label once per link type in this subplot
                legend_label = link_type if (band_name == list(bands_dict.keys())[0] and band_type_name == band_type_names_for_this_subplot[0]) else ""
                ax.barh(current_y_pos_for_plotting, width, left=start_freq, height=0.8, color=colors[link_type], edgecolor='white', linewidth=0.8, label=legend_label) # Changed height to 0.8
                # Frequency Text Label (below the bar)
                ax.text(start_freq + width / 2, current_y_pos_for_plotting - 0.4, f'{start_freq}-{end_freq}', va='top', ha='center', fontsize=7, color='dimgray') # Increased fontsize to 7
            current_y_pos_for_plotting += 1
        current_y_pos_for_plotting += 1 # Add a small gap between band types

    ax.set_xlabel('Frequency (MHz)', fontsize=12)
    ax.set_title(title_text, fontsize=14)
    # Use a softer grid color from seaborn palette
    ax.grid(axis='x', linestyle='--', alpha=0.7, color=sns.color_palette("muted")[7])
    ax.grid(axis='y', linestyle='--', alpha=0.7, color=sns.color_palette("muted")[7])

    # Set custom y-ticks and labels
    ax.set_yticks(y_tick_positions)
    ax.set_yticklabels(y_tick_labels, fontsize=9) # Use band IDs as labels, adjusted fontsize
    ax.tick_params(axis='y', left=False) # Remove default tick marks

    # Control x-axis tick frequency
    ax.xaxis.set_major_locator(ticker.MaxNLocator(nbins=num_xticks))

    handles, labels = ax.get_legend_handles_labels()
    by_label = dict(zip(labels, handles))
    if by_label: # Only show legend if there are items
        ax.legend(by_label.values(), by_label.keys(), title='Link Type', loc='upper right', frameon=True, borderpad=1)
    ax.set_xlim(xlim_range[0], xlim_range[1])
    ax.set_ylim(-1, current_y_pos - 1) # Adjust y-limits to fit all bars properly
    sns.despine(ax=ax, top=True, right=True) # Remove top and right spines for cleaner look

# --- First Plot: FR1 Bands ---
# Adjusted figsize for slightly more horizontal space
fig_fr1, (ax1_fr1, ax2_fr1) = plt.subplots(2, 1, figsize=(15, 10), sharex=False, gridspec_kw={'height_ratios': [1.8, 0.6]})

# Plot for FR1-L and FR1-S bands
plot_bands_on_axis(ax1_fr1, ["FR1-L", "FR1-S"], (1400, 2600), '5G NR Band Allocation (FR1-L/S Bands)', num_xticks=5) # Adjusted xlim_range for better focus

# Plot for FR1-Ku band
plot_bands_on_axis(ax2_fr1, ["FR1-Ku"], (10000, 15000), '5G NR Band Allocation (FR1-Ku Band)', num_xticks=6)

plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

## Waveforms

- Usage of Orthogonal Frequency Division Multiplexing (OFDM) waveform in 5G NR, which is robust against multipath fading and allows for flexible spectrum usage.
- Sub-carrier spacing (SCS) depend on the frequency band:
  - For FR1 (L and S bands): 15 kHz, 30 kHz, 60 kHz
  - For FR1 (Ku band) and FR2 (Ka band): 60 kHz, 120 kHz, 240 kHz
- QAM modulation schemes are used, with higher-order QAM (e.g., up to 1024-QAM in downlink ) providing higher spectral efficiency but requiring better signal quality.
- Different modulations for data transmission and control channels (L1 and L2)

## Multiple access strategies

![source: Perplexity AI](assets/multiple_access.png)

## Multiple access strategies

How different users share the same radio resources:

- **OFDMA** (Orthogonal Frequency Division Multiple Access): Users are allocated different sub-carriers within the same time slot.
- **TDMA** (Time Division Multiple Access): Users are allocated the same frequency band but in different time slots.
- **SDMA** (Space Division Multiple Access): Users are separated by spatial beams.

##  Earth–Platform Geometry: slant range

Slant range, computed from the elevation $\varepsilon$ (note: $R_E$ is the Earth's radius):

$$
\label{eq-slant_range}
d = \sqrt{(R_E + h_{sat})^2 - R_E^2 \cdot \cos^2(\varepsilon)} - R_E \cdot \sin(\varepsilon)
$$

```{python}
#| echo: false
import numpy as np

def compute_slant_range(altitude_km, elevation_angle_deg):
    R_E_km = 6371  # Earth's radius in km
    slant_range_km = np.sqrt((R_E_km + altitude_km)**2 - R_E_km**2 * np.cos(np.radians(elevation_angle_deg))**2) - R_E_km * np.sin(np.radians(elevation_angle_deg))
    return slant_range_km

slant_range_km = compute_slant_range(altitude_km, elevation_angle_deg)
Markdown(f"Slant range (km): {slant_range_km:.2f} km")
```

If we define the two-way latency as $\tau = \frac{2d}{c}$, where $c$ is the speed of light, we can compute the latency for the given slant range.

```{python}
c_km_per_s = 299792.458  # Speed of light in km/s
two_way_latency_s = (2 * slant_range_km) / c_km_per_s
Markdown(f"Two-way latency (ms): {two_way_latency_s * 1000.0:.1f} ms")
```

## Satellite FoV footprint

- See [satellite FoV footprint derivation in the annexes of this deck](#sec-annex_fov_footprint) for the derivation of the footprint radius as a function of satellite altitude and elevation angle.
- Footprint assumes that there is minimum elevation $\varepsilon_{min}$ for the user terminal to communicate with the satellite (see Section 3.3.1 of [@corici2024ntnQos]).

```{python}
import math
import numpy as np
import plotly.graph_objects as go
import pygnss
from pygnss.geodetic import lla_to_xyz, xyz_to_lla



# -----------------------------
# Geometry / FoV computation
# -----------------------------
# Earth radius (mean equatorial radius)
R_E = 6378.137  # km

# Elevation angles (degrees) for boundaries: ε = 0°,2°,4°,6°,8°,10°
elevations_deg = [0, 5, 10]

def compute_perpendicular_unit_vector(a: np.ndarray) -> np.ndarray:
    """
    >>> compute_perpendicular_unit_vector(np.array([1, 0, 0]))
    array([0., 0., 1.])
    """
    a = np.asarray(a, dtype=float)
    if a.shape != (3,):
        raise ValueError("a must be a shape (3,) vector")

    # Choose the axis least aligned with a to avoid tiny cross products
    axes = np.eye(3)
    e = axes[np.argmin(np.abs(a))]  # e is x/y/z axis with smallest |a_i|

    b = np.cross(a, e)
    r_b = np.linalg.norm(b)
    if r_b == 0:
        raise ValueError("Cannot compute a perpendicular vector (a is zero vector).")

    return b / r_b


def compute_boundary_lat_lon(lat_sat_deg, lon_sat_deg, height_sat_km, nadir_angle_deg, n_points=361):
    """
    """

    # Compute the $\gamma$ angle at the Earth center between the subsatellite point and P
    r_s_km = R_E + height_sat_km
    nadir_angle_rad = np.radians(nadir_angle_deg)
    gamma_rad = np.arcsin(r_s_km / R_E * np.sin(nadir_angle_rad)) - nadir_angle_rad

    # Satellite ECEF coordinates
    s = np.array(tuple(lla_to_xyz(lon_sat_deg, lat_sat_deg, height_sat_km)))
    r_s = np.linalg.norm(s)

    u = s / r_s
    k = compute_perpendicular_unit_vector(u)

    e = np.cross(k, u)
    e = e / np.linalg.norm(e)

    n = np.cross(u, e)

    u = u.reshape(3, 1)
    e = e.reshape(3, 1)
    n = n.reshape(3, 1)

    # Create points by varying azimuth around center
    az = np.linspace(0, 2.0 * np.pi, n_points)
    az = az.reshape(1, -1)         # (1, 361)
    cos_az = np.cos(az)            # (1, 361)
    sin_az = np.sin(az)            # (1, 361)

    cos_gamma = np.cos(gamma_rad) # shape should be (1, 361) or (361,)
    sin_gamma = np.sin(gamma_rad)

    p = R_E * 1000.0 * (u * cos_gamma + e * sin_gamma * cos_az + n * sin_gamma * sin_az)
    # p shape: (3, 361)

    xs_m = p[0, :]
    ys_m = p[1, :]
    zs_m = p[2, :]

    lon_deg, lat_deg, _ = xyz_to_lla(xs_m, ys_m, zs_m)

    return lat_deg, lon_deg

def plot_fov_boundaries(lat0_deg, lon0_deg, h, elevations_deg, R_E):
    """
    Generates and displays a Plotly globe visualization of satellite FoV boundaries.

    Args:
        lat0_deg (float): Latitude of the sub-satellite point in degrees.
        lon0_deg (float): Longitude of the sub-satellite point in degrees.
        h (float): Altitude of the satellite above Earth's surface in km.
        elevations_deg (list): List of minimum elevation angles in degrees.
        R_E (float): Earth's radius in km.
    """

    # Hardcoded colors list
    colors = ["#1f77b4", "#ff7f0e", "#2ca02c", "#d62728", "#9467bd", "#8c564b"]

    # Compute maximum nadir angle for all the min elevations
    nadir_max = np.degrees(np.arcsin(R_E/(R_E + h)* np.cos(np.radians(elevations_deg))))

    fig = go.Figure()

    for i, nadir_deg in enumerate(nadir_max):
        lat_curve, lon_curve = compute_boundary_lat_lon(lat0_deg, lon0_deg, h, nadir_deg, n_points=361)
        elev = elevations_deg[i]

        fig.add_trace(
            go.Scattergeo(
                lon=lon_curve,
                lat=lat_curve,
                mode="lines",
                line=dict(width=2, color=colors[i % len(colors)]),
                name=f"ε_min = {elev}º"
            )
        )

    # Sub-satellite point marker
    fig.add_trace(
        go.Scattergeo(
            lon=[lon0_deg],
            lat=[lat0_deg],
            mode="markers",
            marker=dict(size=7, color="black"),
            name="Sub-satellite point"
        )
    )

    fig.update_layout(
        title=f"Satellite FoV Footprint: Lat {lat0_deg}°, Lon {lon0_deg}°, Alt {h} km",
        showlegend=True,
        margin=dict(l=10, r=10, t=50, b=10),
        geo=dict(
            projection_type="equirectangular",
            showland=True,
            landcolor="rgb(240,240,240)",
            showcountries=True,
            showocean=True,
            oceancolor="rgb(210,230,255)",
            showframe=False,
            bgcolor="white",
            lataxis=dict(range=[-90, 90]),
            lonaxis=dict(range=[-180, 180])
        )
    )

    return fig
```

# Session 2 Starlink case study {.use-case-slide background-image="assets/starry_sky.png"}


## Frequency plan {.use-case-slide background-image="assets/starry_sky.png"}

- Downlink signal in 10.7 to 12.7 GHz (Ku band)
- 250 MHz channels
- Spot beams with 2.5° beamwidth
- To avoid interference between spot beams, different frequency channels are used for adjacent beams.
- Effective Isotropic Radiated Power (EIRP) of -56.2 dBW/Hz to -52.8 dBW/Hz
- bidirectional links with user terminals at
X/Ku band[^starlink_fcc_freq_filings] and with gateways at Ka band using left‐handed
or right‐handed circular polarisation (LHCP or RHCP)



- OFDM modulation

See [@humphreys2023signal; @blazquez2024capabilities] for more details on Starlink's radio dimensioning

[^starlink_fcc_freq_filings]: [FCC regulatory filings](https://fcc.report/IBFS/SAT-LOA-20161115-00118) for Starlink's first test Microsat satellites.
